group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: sorted array — find a pair or triple with a given sum
because: Sortedness is the enabling property: moving left can only raise the sum, moving right can only lower it, so each step eliminates a whole row of the search space. Unsorted, this is a hashmap problem instead.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: subarray or substring of a size that is given to you
because: The size is not being searched for, so there is no shrink condition — add the entering element, drop the leaving one.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: longest or shortest subarray such that…, all values non-negative
because: Non-negativity is what makes shrinking sound: extending can only push the sum up, so once the window is invalid, growing it further can never fix it.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: count subarrays summing to exactly k, and negatives are possible
reach_for: Prefix sum + hashmap — a window cannot work
because: Negatives destroy the monotonicity a window needs; extending can lower the sum again, so shrink-while-invalid is unsound. Prefix sums turn “this subarray sums to k” into “have I seen prefix − k before”.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: exactly K distinct / exactly K odd numbers
because: “Exactly” is not directly windowable, but “at most” is monotone in window length, so two at-most passes subtract to exactly.

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: max or min over every window of a fixed size k
because: A heap gives you the max but cannot evict the element that just left the window; a deque kept monotone can drop it in O(1).

group: Window vs prefix sum vs two pointers
says: in-place removal, partition, or reversal over one array
reach_for: Two pointers in the same direction — a slow write index behind a fast read index
because: There is no interval invariant here, so it is not a window at all; nothing is being summed or constrained over a range.

says: return the best value, and you can say why a local choice is safe
because: The test is the exchange argument: can any optimal solution be transformed to agree with your local choice without getting worse? If you cannot state it, you have an answer, not a method — and it will not transfer.

says: a locally worse choice can pay off later
reach_for: DP — and the state must carry whatever the choice affects
because: Greedy fails exactly when choices interact across steps. That interaction is the thing the DP state exists to remember.

says: how many ways / count the arrangements
because: Greedy returns one solution. Counting needs every branch aggregated, which is what a recurrence does.

says: fewest coins or steps to reach a target, denominations arbitrary
because: Largest-first is only safe for canonical coin systems. With arbitrary denominations the greedy choice can strand you short of the target.

says: intervals — keep the most non-overlapping ones
because: Earliest finishing time leaves the most room for everything after it, and that exchange argument is provable. Sorting by start is the merge problem, which is a different question.

says: “with a cooldown”, “at most k transactions”
because: The constraint is a mode you are in rather than a quantity you accumulate — so the states are the modes and the transitions are the actions.

says: return ALL subsets / permutations / valid paths
because: You need the objects themselves, so the output is exponential and no table can compress it.

says: return the COUNT, or the BEST, of those same objects
because: You need only an aggregate, so overlapping subproblems can be collapsed rather than enumerated. Same objects, different question, different technique.

says: shortest path, every edge costs 1
reach_for: BFS — multi-source if there are several origins
because: Uniform cost makes layer order the same as distance order, so first arrival is optimal and no priority queue is needed.

says: shortest path with weights, but at most k hops
reach_for: Bellman–Ford / DP over hop count — NOT Dijkstra
because: Dijkstra finalises a node the first time it is popped, which is wrong once a longer path with fewer hops can still win. The hop limit is a second dimension of state.

says: “minimise the maximum”, “maximise the minimum”, “largest k that still works”
reach_for: Binary search on the answer + a feasibility check
because: The answer is monotone — if k is feasible then everything easier is too — so you search the answer space, not the input.

says: top k from a stream, or n is huge and k is small
because: Sorting is n log n and needs all the data at once; a k-heap is n log k and works on a stream that never fits in memory.

says: prefix matching across many words
because: A hashset answers exact membership only. Prefixes need the shared structure a trie makes explicit.

says: “are these connected”, “merge these groups” — and no path is asked for
because: It answers connectivity without producing a path, which is why it beats BFS/DFS when the merges arrive incrementally.
